catalog_quote: Phonetically, stress is signalled in Bakhtiari by the phonetic lengthening of vowels, increased loudness, and raised pitch. Stress is found on content words (verbs, nouns, adjectives and adverbs), where it is normally hosted by the last syllable of the stem, whatever the number of syllables in the word. 'hars ‘tear(drop)’ ... zah.'le ‘gall bladder’ ... ey.le.'ʋār ‘jaw’ ... Function words, however, are not stressed unless they are emphasized. ... Some affixes are inherently stressed, and others are unstressed (for a list of affixes, and their status with regard to stress, see 2.6.1). If a stressed affix is added to a stem, it takes the word stress; but if the affix is unstressed, stress stays on the stem. ... If there are two stressed suffixes, the second one carries the stress. ... If there is a stressed prefix as well as a stressed suffix, the stressed prefix takes the word stress. ...…
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Persian-type stem-final stress: in content words stress falls on the last syllable of the stem regardless of length ('hars, zah.'le, ey.le.'vār). Affixes are lexically stressed or unstressed: a stressed suffix (definite -(e)ke, plural -gal, vocative -ay, verbal person endings) takes the stress, the last one winning if there are several, so the word is then final-stressed; unstressed suffixes and clitics (object -ne, pronominal clitics, copula -i) leave stress on the stem. Stressed prefixes (imperative be-, negative na-) override stressed suffixes. Function words are unstressed unless emphasized. Stress placement is contrastive in affix-class pairs (di'dom 'I saw' vs 'didom 'he/she saw me'; ton'di 'speed' vs 'tondi 'you are fast'). An alternative provisional coding would be morphological (stem-final default + affix stress classes).
new_statements.exceptions: Function words (vo 'and', men 'in', ayar 'if') unstressed unless emphasized; unstressed affixes/clitics keep stress on the stem; stressed prefixes be-/na- take stress away from stressed suffixes; minimal pairs by affix stress class. Phonetic cues: vowel lengthening, loudness, raised pitch; intonation (§2.5.2) raises pitch on stressed syllables of pragmatically salient words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on morphologically complex words (stem + affixes; clitics attach to a stress-bearing host, §2.4). Data are the Haft Lang Bakhtiari of co-author Ashraf Asadi from the area around Masjed Soleymān, Khuzestān (p. 13-14 of the book). Section 2.5.2 treats sentence intonation separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Anonby & Asadi 2014 describe the Haft Lang Bakhtiari of Masjed Soleymān (Khuzestān), the co-author's own variety; Bakhtiari has three large dialect areas (Masjed Soleymān, Shahr-e Kord/Chahar Mahal, Lorestan side) and the 2025 Bavadi article notes vowel-inventory variation across them, but no source examined suggests the stress rule differs. Glottocode bakh1245 covers all.

new_statements.quote: [p. 94] For Bakhtiari, a phonological word is most appropriately defined as any element in a string of speech that is both pronounceable on its own and capable of carrying stress (or, more precisely, the accent of the phonological phrase; see Anonby & Taheri-Ardali 2018, section 2.3). [p. 104] ... the parts are fully joined, since only a single stressed syllable – that of the suffix – is possible for the word. [p. 152] In addition, whereas subject clitics are normally unstressed, verbal suffixes carry stress by default (i.e., unless they are overridden by a stressed prefix – see Anonby & Asadi 2014:65–66 – or topic-related emphasis on the verb root).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's final-syllable record and with the 2014 statement it cites; adds that verbal suffixes are stressed by default, that subject clitics, ezāfe and demonstrative -o are unstressed, that a stressed prefix wins over the suffix, and that the stress is better described as the accent of the phonological phrase. No new general rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The orthography volume states no general placement rule of its own; it defers to Anonby & Asadi 2014:65-66 and to Anonby & Taheri-Ardali 2018 §2.3. What it does say is compatible with final (suffix-final) stress: a word has only one stressed syllable, and in fully-joined reduplicated forms it is the word-final derivational suffix (-e, -ak); verbal person suffixes carry stress by default unless a stressed prefix or topic emphasis on the root overrides them. It also reframes word stress as, 'more precisely, the accent of the phonological phrase'. Reading given with low confidence because the rule is inferred from suffix behaviour, not stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed elements: subject clitics (copula) -om, -i, -e, -im, -in, -en (p. 140); the ezāfe -e, the unstressed 3sg copula -e and the unstressed demonstrative suffix -o (pp. 67, 138). Verbal suffix stress is overridden by a stressed prefix or by topic-related emphasis on the verb root (p. 152). Reduplicated stems without a suffix are two phonological words, each able to carry (phrasal) accent (p. 103).
new_statements.identity_note: Zolfaghari 2017 describes the Haft Lang Bakhtiari of the Hamule (Hamuleh) tribal group ('I only focus on the Hamule version of Bakhtiari to which I feel most affinity', p. 223 fn.), and cites Moradi's examples from other varieties. Anonby & Asadi 2014/2018 describe the Masjed Soleymān Haft Lang variety of co-author Asadi. Both are Haft Lang; no dialect-specific stress difference is reported.

new_statements.quote: [p. 220, fn. 219] The mark (‘) indicates that the following syllable is stressed, but as Bakhtiari words are canonically stressed on the final syllable, I will only indicate the stress when it deviates from the default rule. [p. 223] This specific stressed definite suffix only marks a noun in an adjectival compound: [p. 224] The third way of marking indefiniteness is to add the unstressed suffix -i right after the same word which is already a qualified indefinite noun [...] [p. 267] It is formed by attaching an unstressed suffix -e or by -ø [...] to the end of the past stem. [...] The present participle is formed by attaching a stressed suffix -a to the present stem.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final syllable) and as Anonby & Asadi 2014. Framing differs slightly: Anonby & Asadi say last syllable of the stem with some inherently stressed affixes; Zolfaghari says word-final by default with a short list of unstressed suffixes. Both descriptions yield the same surface positions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls by default on the final syllable of the word; the author marks stress in transcription only where it deviates from that default. Deviations named: the indefinite suffix -i and the past-participle suffix -e are unstressed (so stress stays on the stem-final syllable before them), whereas the definite suffix -e and the present-participle suffix -a are stressed. Stated in a footnote, not in a phonology section.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed suffixes: indefinite -i (p. 224), past-participle -e/-ø (p. 267), Yarshater's euphonic -a/-e cited as unstressed (p. 275 fn. 262). Stressed suffixes: definite -e in adjectival compounds (p. 223), present-participle -a (p. 267).
new_statements.identity_note: Zolfaghari 2017 describes the Haft Lang Bakhtiari of the Hamule (Hamuleh) tribal group ('I only focus on the Hamule version of Bakhtiari to which I feel most affinity', p. 223 fn.), and cites Moradi's examples from other varieties. Anonby & Asadi 2014/2018 describe the Masjed Soleymān Haft Lang variety of co-author Asadi. Both are Haft Lang; no dialect-specific stress difference is reported.
